🥘 Ingredients

  • 2 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil
  • 4 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
  • 1 can (28 ounces) crushed tomatoes
  • 1 teaspoon salt
  • 1/2 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper
  • 1 teaspoon dried oregano
  • 1 teaspoon sugar (optional)
  • Fresh basil leaves for garnish (optional)

👩‍🍳 Instructions

  1. Heat the olive oil in a medium saucepan over medium heat until shimmering but not smoking. Add the thinly sliced garlic and gently sauté for 1-2 minutes, stirring often to prevent burning. This step is crucial because the garlic infuses the oil with flavor, creating a fragrant base for the sauce. Watch closely—the garlic should turn golden but not brown, as burnt garlic will taste bitter and ruin the sauce. The slow release of garlic flavor into the oil sets the tone for the entire sauce.
  2. Pour in the crushed tomatoes carefully, stirring to combine with the garlic and oil. Add salt, pepper, oregano, and sugar if using. Bring the sauce to a gentle simmer over medium-low heat. This gradual heating allows the flavors to meld without breaking down the tomatoes too quickly. Rushing this step can cause the sauce to taste raw or overly acidic. Once simmering, reduce the heat to low to maintain a gentle bubble—it should not boil vigorously.
  3. Let the sauce simmer uncovered over low heat for 25-30 minutes, stirring occasionally. This slow simmer is what transforms the sauce—water evaporates, flavors concentrate, and the sauce thickens to a luscious texture. Stirring prevents sticking and ensures even cooking. Avoid covering the pot, as trapping moisture will keep the sauce watery. If you see the sauce thickening unevenly or sticking, lower the heat slightly or add a splash of water.
  4. Taste the sauce and adjust seasoning if needed—more salt, pepper, or a pinch of sugar to balance acidity. This step is important because canned tomatoes vary in sweetness and acidity. Tasting lets you personalize the sauce to your preference. If the sauce feels too thick, add a tablespoon or two of water and stir well.
  5. Remove the sauce from heat and stir in fresh basil leaves if you like. The residual heat will release the basil’s aroma without cooking it harshly. This adds a fresh, herbal note that brightens the sauce. If you prefer a smoother texture, use an immersion blender to lightly puree the sauce to your liking.
  6. Serve hot over your favorite pasta, or use as a base for dishes like meatballs or eggplant parmesan. The sauce pairs well with any type of pasta but is especially great with spaghetti or penne. If not using immediately, cool to room temperature before storing in an airtight container.
  7. To store leftovers, transfer cooled sauce into an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 4 days. Reheat gently on the stove or microwave, adding a splash of water or olive oil to refresh the texture. Avoid boiling again to preserve flavor.
  8. For freezing, portion the cooled sauce into freezer-safe containers or bags, leaving some headspace for expansion. Freeze for up to 3 months. Thaw overnight in the fridge before reheating gently.
  9. If you want a chunkier sauce, avoid blending and use whole peeled tomatoes instead of crushed. Crush them by hand or with a spoon in the pot to keep texture. This variation adds a rustic feel and works well for hearty dishes.

  • 1/4 cup chopped fresh basil
  • 1/4 teaspoon black pepper

👩‍🍳 Instructions

  1. Preheat your oven to 375°F (190°C). Roll out the pie crust and fit it into a 9-inch pie pan. Press the crust gently into the edges and prick the bottom a few times with a fork to prevent bubbling during baking. Blind bake the crust for about 10 minutes to get it partially cooked; this helps keep it crisp when we add the juicy tomatoes later. Make sure the crust is lightly golden but not fully browned at this stage, or it may burn in the final bake.
  2. While the crust bakes, slice your ripe tomatoes about 1/4 inch thick. Lay the slices on paper towels and sprinkle them evenly with 1 teaspoon of salt. Let them sit for 10-15 minutes to draw out excess moisture. This step is crucial because it prevents the pie from becoming soggy and concentrates the tomato flavor. After resting, gently pat the slices dry with more paper towels to remove the released liquid.
  3. In a medium bowl, combine the mayonnaise, shredded cheddar, mozzarella, Parmesan, chopped basil, and black pepper. Mix until well blended. This creamy cheese mixture is the heart of the pie, adding richness and a melty texture that contrasts wonderfully with the fresh tomatoes. Don’t skip the basil—it brightens the flavors and adds a fresh, herbaceous note.
  4. Arrange a single layer of the tomato slices over the partially baked crust. Spread about half of the cheese mixture evenly over the tomatoes. Then add another layer of tomatoes and top with the remaining cheese mixture. Layering like this ensures every bite has a balance of tomato and creamy cheese, creating a beautiful texture and flavor contrast.
  5. Place the pie back into the oven and bake at 375°F (190°C) for 30 minutes. During baking, the cheese mixture melts and browns slightly, while the tomatoes soften but hold their shape. This baking time allows the crust to finish cooking and become golden and flaky. Keep an eye on the crust edges; if they brown too quickly, loosely cover with foil to prevent burning.
  6. Once baked, remove the pie from the oven and let it cool for at least 15 minutes before slicing. Cooling helps the filling set so the slices hold together nicely. If you cut it too soon, the filling may be too soft and runny. The pie should be warm but firm with a flaky crust and a creamy, cheesy tomato topping.
  7. For serving, garnish with a few fresh basil leaves if you like. This adds a pop of color and a fresh herbal aroma that complements the savory pie. Serve it alongside a crisp green salad or enjoy it on its own for a light meal. It’s also fantastic at room temperature, making it great for picnics or potlucks.
  8. If you want to prepare ahead, you can assemble the pie and store it uncovered in the fridge for up to 12 hours before baking. Just be sure the tomato slices are well drained to avoid sogginess. Bring the pie to room temperature before baking to ensure even cooking.
  9. To reheat leftover tomato pie, warm it in a 350°F (175°C) oven for 10-15 minutes until heated through and the crust is crisp again. Avoid microwaving as it can make the crust soggy. A splash of water on a pan while reheating helps keep the filling moist without drying out.

  4. Place the crackers in small piles around the cheeses. Whole grain crackers add crunch and a nice contrast to the soft cheese and juicy fruit. Avoid crushed crackers by placing them gently and not stacking too high. This also makes it easy for kids to grab individual crackers.
  5. Add the fruit next, distributing grapes, apple slices, and baby carrots evenly across the board. Mixing colors and shapes keeps the board visually interesting and encourages kids to try different items. Be sure to space fruit so it doesn’t get squished or lose its shape.
  6. If using dips like hummus or peanut butter, place them in small bowls and set them on the board. These add flavor variety and are great for dipping crackers or veggies. Make sure the bowls are stable and won’t tip over easily. This helps keep the board tidy and fun.
  7. Add any fun extras you want like pretzels, small pickles, or cherry tomatoes to fill gaps and add texture. These extras make the board feel more special and give kids more choices to explore. Avoid overcrowding, though, so the board stays easy to navigate.
  8. Give the board a quick once-over to remove any bruised fruit or broken crackers. Presentation counts, especially with kids! A tidy, colorful board invites them to dig in. If anything looks off, swap it out before serving.
  9. Serve immediately or cover loosely with plastic wrap and refrigerate if preparing ahead. Serving right away keeps everything fresh and crunchy. If stored, bring to room temperature before serving to restore flavors and textures.

🍳 Cook Time: 30 minutes

⏰ Total Time: N/A minutes

🍽️ Servings: 4

📊 Difficulty: Medium

🥘 Ingredients

  • 1 medium napa cabbage (about 2 pounds), chopped
  • 1/4 cup sea salt
  • 4 cups water
  • 1 tablespoon grated ginger
  • 4 cloves garlic, minced
  • 2 teaspoons sugar
  • 3 tablespoons Korean red pepper flakes (gochugaru)
  • 4 green onions, sliced
  • 1 small carrot, julienned
  • 2 tablespoons fish sauce

👩‍🍳 Instructions

  1. Start by chopping the napa cabbage into bite-sized pieces. Place it in a large bowl and sprinkle the sea salt evenly over the cabbage. Toss well to coat each piece. Then, pour in 4 cups of cold water to cover the cabbage. The salt draws moisture out, which softens the cabbage and helps create the ideal texture for fermentation. Leave it to soak for at least 2 hours, tossing every 30 minutes to ensure even salting. Avoid skimping on this step, as under-salting can lead to soggy kimchi or poor fermentation.
  2. While the cabbage is salting, prepare the kimchi paste. In a small bowl, combine the grated ginger, minced garlic, sugar, Korean red pepper flakes, and fish sauce. Mix until you get a thick, vibrant paste. This paste is the flavor powerhouse — the ginger and garlic add warmth, the gochugaru brings heat and color, and the fish sauce gives that umami depth. Be sure to mix thoroughly so the sugar dissolves, which balances the spicy and sour notes during fermentation.
  3. After the cabbage has soaked, rinse it thoroughly under cold water at least twice to remove excess salt. Then, drain it well using a colander, pressing lightly to remove extra water but don’t squeeze too hard or the cabbage will lose its crunch. This rinsing step is crucial because if too salty, the kimchi can become overly salty and inhibit fermentation. Once drained, transfer the cabbage back to the large bowl.
  4. Add the prepared kimchi paste to the cabbage along with the sliced green onions and julienned carrot. Using clean hands (wear gloves if you prefer), mix everything thoroughly until every piece of cabbage is coated evenly with the spicy paste. This ensures consistent flavor and proper fermentation. Don’t rush — take your time mixing to distribute the paste well. This step also helps break down the cabbage slightly for better texture.
  5. Pack the kimchi mixture tightly into a clean glass jar or fermentation container. Press down firmly to remove air pockets, leaving about 1 inch of space at the top for expansion during fermentation. Air exposure can cause spoilage, so packing tightly is key to a successful ferment. Seal the jar with a lid but don’t screw it on too tight — gases need to escape to prevent pressure buildup.
  6. Leave the jar at room temperature (around 65-75°F) to ferment for 1-2 days. The warmer your kitchen, the faster the fermentation. During this time, the flavors develop and the cabbage softens while gaining that signature tang. Check daily, gently pressing down to keep the cabbage submerged in its brine. If you see bubbles or hear a slight fizz, that’s a good sign fermentation is active. Avoid opening the jar too often as oxygen can interfere with the process.
  7. After fermenting at room temperature, move the jar to the refrigerator to slow fermentation and develop flavor further. Cold storage keeps the kimchi crisp and lets the flavors mellow over the next week or more. You can eat it right away or let it mature for deeper complexity. Refrigeration also helps preserve the probiotics longer. Always use a clean utensil to scoop out kimchi to avoid contamination.
  8. Before serving, give the kimchi a gentle stir to mix the brine and flavors. It’s fantastic as a side dish with rice, grilled meats, or mixed into soups and stews. If you want it spicier, add extra red pepper flakes when mixing the paste. For milder kimchi, reduce the gochugaru. Experiment a bit to find your favorite heat level!
  9. If you want to speed up fermentation, you can leave the kimchi at room temperature for up to 3 days, but monitor closely to avoid over-fermentation which leads to mushy texture and overly sour taste. Also, always store kimchi in a glass or food-grade plastic container to avoid metallic flavors from reacting with the acids produced during fermentation.
